# Passwords, MFA and identity: Governing one risk {#sec-18-passwords-mfa-and-identity}

Chapter 17 accepted R1's residual on a condition --- that MFA lands and stays
landed --- and this chapter makes good on it by governing the risk behind the
course's most-used example completely, end to end. Authentication is the right
subject for the exercise twice over: It is where FastGoods' account-takeover
risk actually lives, and it is the rare control area with a documented
forty-year history of official advice being issued, backfiring, and being
formally reversed --- so it teaches both a control and a lesson about rules. The
chapter runs the attack paths behind account takeover, the strange history of
the password rules, what modern governance actually requires, MFA and the
passkeys now replacing passwords, and the identity and access discipline beyond
the login --- and it ends where a governed risk should: The policy written, the
register row closed, and the metrics watching.

## Why passwords fail {#sec-18-why-passwords-fail}

The password's failure mode is not weakness but *reuse*. People hold far more
accounts than memories, so the same password serves many sites --- and then one
breach anywhere unlocks accounts everywhere, because attackers feed the leaked
pairs into every login page that will take them. A strong password leaked from a
gaming forum still opens FastGoods' shop if there is no second factor: That
chain --- breached elsewhere, reused here --- is R1 at its root, and it has a
name.

::: {#def-credstuffing}
## Credential stuffing

Credential stuffing is the automated trying of username--password pairs leaked
from one service against the login pages of others, exploiting the human habit
of reuse. It is the leading path to account takeover, and it defeats password
*strength* entirely: The password being tried is the real one.
:::

Every takeover travels one of three main paths, and each is broken by a
different control --- so knowing the path tells you which control you are
actually buying (@tbl-attackpaths). Credential stuffing is broken by
uniqueness and by MFA; guessing and cracking by length and breached-list checks;
and phishing --- the user tricked into typing the password onto a fake page
(Chapter 14's craft) --- is only reliably broken by *phishing-resistant* MFA, a
distinction this chapter sharpens in @sec-18-mfa-and-passkeys. One more
inherited failure completes the picture: Complexity rules meant to prevent
guessing instead taught everyone the same predictable patterns --- `Password1!`
satisfies most of them --- which is the first clue that the rules themselves
have a history worth examining.

::: {#tbl-attackpaths}
  **Path**              **How it works**                           **What breaks it**
  --------------------- ------------------------------------------ ------------------------------
  Credential stuffing   Leaked pairs from other sites tried here   Unique passwords; MFA
  Phishing              The user is tricked into typing it         Phishing-resistant MFA
  Guessing / cracking   Weak or common passwords brute-forced      Length; breached-list checks

  : Three paths to an account takeover, each broken by a different control. R1
  is the first path --- and note that ordinary MFA breaks stuffing and guessing,
  but only phishing-resistant MFA reliably breaks the second row.
:::

## A short history of the rules {#sec-18-a-short-history-of-the-rules}

Password governance is old enough to have made, institutionalised and reversed a
large mistake, and the timeline explains why so many corporate policies still
enforce advice its own author regrets (@fig-pwtimeline). Passwords
entered computing with MIT's time-sharing systems in the early 1960s; the first
mass demonstration of their weakness came in 1988, when the Morris worm spread
through the young internet partly by guessing weak passwords from a small
dictionary. The rules era began in 2003: NIST guidance written by Bill Burr
mandated composition rules --- upper, lower, digit, symbol --- and rotation
every ninety days, and the advice hardened into audit checklists and login
screens worldwide for fourteen years. The reversal came in 2017: NIST SP
800-63B, the current digital-identity guideline, dropped forced rotation and
composition rules in favour of length, uniqueness and screening against
known-breached passwords --- and Burr, by then retired, told interviewers
plainly that he regretted much of the 2003 advice. From 2018 the FIDO2 and
WebAuthn standards, joined by the platform vendors' passkey rollout from 2022,
began replacing the password itself.

![Forty years of password advice. The complexity-and-rotation era lasted from 2003 to 2017 before the evidence caught up with it; the current era favours length, uniqueness and blocklists --- and increasingly no password at all.](figures/fig-pwtimeline.svg){#fig-pwtimeline}

Why did the old rules backfire? Because they optimised for a password that
*looks* strong to a checker, not for human behaviour --- and Chapter 14
predicted the rest. Forced ninety-day changes produced small predictable tweaks:
`Spring2024` duly became `Spring2025`, and an attacker who has one iteration can
guess the next. Composition rules produced the same substitutions everyone uses,
so cracking dictionaries simply learned them. And the accumulated friction
produced exactly the workarounds the usable-security literature documents:
Reuse, sticky notes, and weaker choices made in frustration. People routed
around security that fought the way they work --- rationally. Britain's NCSC
reversed its advice on the same evidence, and the episode deserves its place in
a governance course for the general lesson: A rule that ignores behaviour does
not produce the behaviour; it produces theatre plus workarounds, at full cost
and negative benefit.

## Modern password governance {#sec-18-modern-password-governance}

What good rules look like now fits in two short lists, both traceable to SP
800-63B and to Jøsang's treatment (Ch. 8). *Do*: Favour long passphrases over
cryptic strings --- length beats complexity, and four unrelated words are both
stronger and more memorable than `P@ssw0rd`; check new passwords against lists
of known-breached passwords, which removes exactly the candidates stuffing and
cracking try first; and require a unique password per site, which is what
actually breaks credential stuffing. *Avoid*: Forced periodic changes; mandatory
symbol-and-number composition; and password hints or security questions, which
are just weaker passwords with public answers. One practical fact makes the "do"
list livable: Uniqueness at scale is impossible from memory, so the *password
manager* is where policy meets practice. Jøsang describes the three types ---
built into the operating system, built into the browser, and third-party
applications --- all keeping an encrypted vault, often cloud-synchronised, and
his governance point is the one that belongs in a policy: The vault concentrates
everything, so it is protected with a strong passphrase and high-strength MFA of
its own (§§8.3--8.4, pp. 165 ff.). A company that mandates unique strong
passwords without providing a manager has written Chapter 14's workaround into
its own policy.

## MFA and passkeys {#sec-18-mfa-and-passkeys}

Authentication verifies that a user is who they claim, and every method is built
from three kinds of factor --- Jøsang's knowledge-, ownership- and
biometric-based authenticators (Ch. 8): Something you *know* (a password or PIN
--- stealable, guessable), something you *have* (a phone or security key ---
must be physically held), something you *are* (a fingerprint or face).

::: {#def-mfa}
## Multi-factor authentication

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires two or more *different* factors used
together --- typically something known plus something held. A stolen password
alone then no longer opens the account, which removes the decisive weakness
behind credential stuffing; Jøsang (§8.6) treats authentication by two or more
simultaneous methods as the definition of 2FA/MFA. It is cheap to enable and the
single biggest authentication win available.
:::

Not all second factors are equal, though, and the differences decide what a
policy should require where (@tbl-mfarank). An SMS code can be captured
by SIM-swapping the phone number, and --- like any code --- typed by the victim
into a convincing fake site. An authenticator app's rotating code (TOTP) removes
the SIM problem but can still be phished live: The fake page asks for the code
and relays it within its thirty seconds. A FIDO2 security key or passkey resists
the phish structurally: The credential is cryptographic and bound to the genuine
site's origin, so there is nothing to retype and nothing a fake site can
usefully ask for.

::: {#def-passkey}
## Passkey

A passkey is a cryptographic credential (FIDO2/WebAuthn) stored on the user's
device and bound to the legitimate site it was created for. Login is a signature
exchange, not a shared secret: Nothing is typed, nothing can be reused
elsewhere, and a counterfeit site cannot ask for anything useful --- which is
what "phishing-resistant MFA" means in practice.
:::

::: {#tbl-mfarank}
  **Method**                       **Weakness**                                **Phishing resistance**
  -------------------------------- ------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------
  SMS code                         SIM swap; typed into fake sites             [**Low**]{style="color: riskHigh"}
  Authenticator app (TOTP)         Code can be phished live                    [**Medium**]{style="color: riskMod"}
  Security key / passkey (FIDO2)   Bound to the real site; nothing to retype   [**High**]{style="color: riskLow"}

  : Not all MFA is equal. Any MFA defeats credential stuffing; only the last row
  reliably defeats phishing --- which is why policies grade the requirement by
  account sensitivity.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Real-world case: Uber (2022): MFA, fatigued

In September 2022 an attacker bought a contractor's leaked credentials, then met
Uber's MFA --- and simply pushed through it: Repeated login attempts flooded the
contractor's phone with approval prompts (*MFA fatigue*), followed by a WhatsApp
message posing as IT support asking them to accept "to make the notifications
stop". One tap later the attacker was inside --- where a network share yielded a
script with hardcoded administrator credentials for the privileged-access
system, turning one contractor's login into keys across the company. The case
compresses this chapter: Stuffing supplied the password; push-prompt MFA fell to
social engineering, exactly the human channel Chapter 14 mapped;
phishing-resistant factors and number-matching prompts exist to close that
channel; and the blast radius came from a least-privilege failure --- the
credentials lying where any account could read them. MFA is the single biggest
win, and the case is why the *kind* of MFA, and what an account can reach
afterwards, are policy questions rather than details.
:::

## IAM, the policy, and closing the row {#sec-18-iam-the-policy-and-closing-the}

Beyond the login lies the question authentication cannot answer: What may this
identity *do*? That is identity and access management --- Jøsang gives it a
chapter of its own (Ch. 9, pp. 191 ff.) --- and its two working rules the course
has been circling since Block III. *The lifecycle*: Access is granted on
joining, changed on moving, removed on leaving --- the joiner--mover--leaver
process where most orphaned access is born, root-caused in Chapter 8 and drilled
in Chapters 14 and 16. *Least privilege*: Each identity gets only the access its
role needs, because privilege that exists only to be convenient is blast radius
waiting for a takeover --- the lesson Uber's hardcoded administrator credentials
teach at scale. Privileged accounts get the strict end of every rule:
Phishing-resistant MFA and extra monitoring, because they are where a takeover
stops being an incident and becomes the incident.

Governance means writing it down, and the whole chapter compresses into a
one-page authentication policy --- Chapter 15's hierarchy applied, with the
graded MFA requirement as its signature feature (@tbl-authpolicy).

::: {#tbl-authpolicy}
  **Requirement**       **Rule**
  --------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------
  MFA                   Required on all accounts reaching customer or admin data
  Passwords             Long passphrases; breached-list checks; no forced rotation
  Access                Least privilege; reviewed when roles change
  Joiners / leavers     Access granted and revoked promptly
  Privileged accounts   Phishing-resistant MFA (passkey or key); extra monitoring

  : FastGoods' authentication policy on one page: Enforceable, tied to real
  systems, and graded --- ordinary MFA for everyone, phishing-resistant for the
  privileged.
:::

And with the policy written and MFA landed, R1's register row --- opened in
Chapter 8, treated in Chapter 10, decided and reported in Chapter 17 --- is
updated and closed (@tbl-r1close). This is what "governing a risk end to
end" looks like on paper, and the pattern, not the password, is the chapter's
real product: Any risk you will ever own travels the same road.

::: {#tbl-r1close}
  -------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Risk**       R1 --- Account takeover via reused passwords
  **Controls**   MFA on all accounts (A.8.5); modern password rules; breached-list checks
  **Residual**   [**Low**]{style="color: riskLow"} --- was [**high**]{style="color: riskCrit"} inherent
  **Status**     Accepted (Chapter 17's record); KRIs on the dashboard; review in 12 months
  -------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  : R1's register row, closed: Assessed (Chapter 8), treated (Chapter 10),
  decided and reported (Chapter 17), governed and measured (this chapter). One
  risk has now travelled the whole course.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Finding the risk: In the identity data

The account list is a risk register that maintains itself --- read it quarterly,
backwards. Accounts with no login for ninety days are leavers the process missed
or access nobody needs; shared accounts are accountability already lost (whose
action was it?); the count of administrator accounts is a blast-radius number
that only ever drifts upward; accounts exempt from MFA are R1's remaining
doorway, each one a decision someone should have signed (Chapter 17); and
privileged accounts still on SMS or push MFA are @tbl-mfarank's middle
rows guarding the top prizes. Every line item converts directly into a register
entry or an access review --- the cheapest audit FastGoods will ever run.
:::

::: {#exm-studentauth}
## The student's own authentication audit

Run this chapter on yourself in twenty minutes. Count the accounts sharing your
most-used password --- that number is your personal credential-stuffing
exposure. Then protect the one account that unlocks the rest: Your *email*,
because every "forgot password" flow routes through it --- MFA there first, a
passkey if offered. Then adopt a manager and let it generate unique passphrases
as you touch each account, highest-value first: Bank, studies, cloud drive (the
thesis, again). No rotation calendar, no symbol gymnastics --- the modern rules,
applied to the identity you actually own. The exercise is R1's governance in
miniature, minus the committee.
:::

##### Reading for this chapter.

Jøsang, Chapter 8 (user authentication: Factors, password practice, managers,
MFA, pp. 165 ff., especially §§8.3--8.4 and §8.6) and Chapter 9 (identity and
access management, pp. 191 ff.); NIST SP 800-63B (the 2017 digital-identity
guideline behind the modern rules --- skim the password section and notice what
is absent). Both books are available in the library and on the Canvas course
page.

## Summary {#sec-18-summary}

Passwords fail through reuse before weakness: Credential stuffing
(@def-credstuffing) replays leaked pairs at scale, and the three
takeover paths --- stuffing, phishing, guessing --- are each broken by a
different control (@tbl-attackpaths). The rules have a history that
explains the mess: Composition-and-rotation doctrine from 2003 backfired into
predictable patterns and workarounds, was formally reversed by NIST SP 800-63B
in 2017 --- its own author repentant --- and is being outgrown by FIDO2 and
passkeys; the governance lesson is that rules which ignore behaviour buy
theatre. Modern rules are short: Length over complexity, uniqueness,
breached-list checks, no forced rotation, no hints --- made livable by a
password manager whose vault gets a strong passphrase and strong MFA of its own.
MFA (@def-mfa) is the single biggest win, but the factors are graded:
SMS low, TOTP medium, and only origin-bound passkeys (@def-passkey)
phishing-resistant --- the distinction Uber's MFA-fatigue breach turned into a
headline. Beyond the login, IAM governs what identities may do: The
joiner--mover--leaver lifecycle and least privilege bound the blast radius,
privileged accounts get the strict tier, and the whole chapter compresses into a
one-page policy (@tbl-authpolicy) --- after which R1's register row
closes (@tbl-r1close): Assessed, treated, decided, governed, watched.

FastGoods has now governed its own riskiest control end to end. What Block V
still owes is the risk that no internal control reaches --- the suppliers, the
cloud, the chain of parties FastGoods depends on and does not run. Lecture 19
closes the block outside the walls.

## Self-check {#sec-18-self-check}

Try these before the next lecture.

::: {#exr-18-name-the-path}
## Name the path

For each incident, name the attack path of @tbl-attackpaths and the one
control that would have broken it: (a) A FastGoods customer's shop account is
opened with a password from an unrelated forum breach. (b) A clerk types their
password and TOTP code into a pixel-perfect fake login page. (c) An attacker's
script works through the 10,000 most common passwords against the admin login.
:::

::: {#exr-18-audit-the-policy}
## Audit the policy

A company policy reads: "Passwords: Minimum 8 characters, at least one
uppercase, digit and symbol; changed every 90 days; security questions for
recovery." Rewrite it to SP 800-63B-era rules, and justify each change in one
clause.
:::

::: {#exr-18-grade-the-factors}
## Grade the factors

FastGoods can roll out SMS codes, TOTP apps, or passkeys. Assign a factor to (a)
customer accounts and (b) the two admin accounts, using @tbl-mfarank,
and defend the split in three sentences --- including why the answer for (b) is
not merely "the same as (a)".
:::

::: {#exr-18-read-the-breach}
## Read the breach

Using the Uber case, name the three distinct control failures in order of
occurrence, and for each the chapter section whose guidance addresses it.
:::
